What it is there: A many-headed reptile of the Lair and Swamp; slashing attacks sever heads, which regrow unless the stump is burned.

Name: Royal Jelly
Goal: Defeat a boss guarding a treasure vault
Why this pairing: The Slime Pits' boss sits in front of a guaranteed treasure vault and the slimy rune; that pairing, a guardian and its hoard, is everywhere. A second slime boss for the slime tag.
What it is there: The jelly boss of Slime:5: huge HP, acid, and every time it's damaged it spawns other jellies.

Name: Gharbad the Weak
Goal: Spare an enemy that begs for its life
Why this pairing: Gharbad begs to be spared and promises a reward, then turns on you. Sparing an enemy is a choice many games offer (Undertale onwards), and it's his whole story.
What it is there: A unique Flesh Clan goatman on level 4 who offers a reward in exchange for his life, then attacks after a few visits.

Name: Fallen One
Goal: Make a group of enemies flee
Why this pairing: Fallen attack in swarms but scatter in panic when one of them dies, which every Diablo player remembers. Routing a group works in any game where enemies can flee; it pairs with the Terrified status candidate.
What it is there: Small imps that attack in large groups and run away in fear when one of their number is killed.

Name: Archbishop Lazarus
Goal: Defeat a boss inside a church, temple or cathedral
Why this pairing: The traitor priest who led Tristram's people to the Butcher waits in the deepest part of the cathedral's underworld. Churches and temples are common settings in action roguelikes. With Leoric and the Butcher he makes Diablo's three bosses.
What it is there: The corrupted archbishop who lured the townsfolk to their deaths; fought at the end of his own quest, teleporting and summoning.

Name: Hound
Goal: Survive a wave of enemies that arrives on a timer
Why this pairing: The growling that warns a hound attack is coming is Don't Starve's clock. Timed waves are in survivors-likes, tower defence and roguelites alike.
What it is there: Packs that attack every 3-13 days, announced by growling, bigger as the game goes on.

Name: Werepig
Goal: Defeat an enemy at night or under a full moon
Why this pairing: Pigs turn into Werepigs at the full moon. A day/night clock is common, and night fights are a natural Feat. ('Witness an enemy transform' is already a Streets of Rogue candidate, so the night is the goal, not the change.)
What it is there: Pigs become hostile Werepigs during a full moon or after eating too much monster meat.

Name: Tentacle
Goal: Cross a swamp or marsh without getting hit
Why this pairing: Tentacles hide under the marsh and lash out at whatever walks past; the marsh is the danger, so crossing it untouched is the goal. ('Defeat an enemy that burrows' is a Risk of Rain candidate.)
What it is there: Hidden in Marshes and Caves; the ground bubbles before one bursts up and attacks.

Name: Ancient Guardian
Goal: Make a charging enemy crash into a wall
Why this pairing: The Guardian charges like a Clockwork Rook, and the way to beat it is to make it hit the walls. Dodging a charge into terrain is an action-game staple. Don't Starve's bosses are now two: Deerclops and the Guardian.
What it is there: The boss of the Ruins' Labyrinth: 2500 Health, charges at the player.

Name: Hag
Goal: Rescue an ally that an enemy has captured
Why this pairing: The Hag's fight is her cooking pot: she throws a hero in and you have to get them out. Rescuing a captured ally is common in party games. With the Collector and the Shambler she makes Darkest Dungeon's three bosses.
What it is there: The Weald's boss: her pot takes the front ranks, and heroes thrown into it cook until rescued.
Clones: Mini U.F.O. (Atomicrops): abducts your farm animals rather than a hero, and each one taken comes back as an Alien Pod enemy

Name: Carp
Goal: Get hurt by something that looked harmless
Why this pairing: The killer carp is one of the game's most famous legends: older versions made them savage. The wiki notes that current carp are benign, so the joke is the history. Any game has its harmless-looking hazard.
What it is there: Freshwater fish in groups of 5-10; infamous in earlier versions for their aggression and powerful bite, an inconvenience at worst today.

Name: Shamura
Goal: Defeat a boss that never stops chasing you
Why this pairing: Shamura, the eldest Bishop, rushes the Lamb and stays glued to them, with spiders bursting from webs. Being hounded is a common boss pattern. With Leshy and the live One Who Waits, Cult of the Lamb's three bosses.
What it is there: The oldest Bishop, ruler of the Silk Cradle: a purple spider, the most aggressive boss in the game. 'Five becomes four becomes three becomes two becomes one becomes nothing.'

Name: The Hangman
Goal: Win a fight before a countdown on you runs out
Why this pairing: The Hangman marks a hero for death: the mark kills in a few turns unless the fight is won (or fled). Racing a death timer is a goal many games host. Pairs with the Doomed status candidate.
What it is there: A creature with the Death Mark ability: a marked character dies 2-4 moves later unless the battle is won first.

Name: The Golem King
Goal: Dodge an attack you can only see coming by its shadow
Why this pairing: The Golem King's stone fist drops from above and the shadow is the only warning; reading shadows is an action staple. ('A boss that never moves' is already Gurdy's goal, so the shadow is his.)
What it is there: The Golem Dungeon's boss: an immobile giant boulder whose flying stone hand smashes down where its shadow falls.

Name: Carnivorous Mutae
Goal: Defeat a boss after clearing every minion it planted
Why this pairing: The Mutae plants spore-spitting plants around the arena, and clearing them first is the recommended strategy. A boss with adds is everywhere.
What it is there: The Forest Dungeon's boss: a massive carnivorous plant that plants spitting minions, roots the floor with spikes and poisons on touch.

Name: Stevari
Goal: Anger the guards by breaking something you shouldn't
Why this pairing: Stevari ('Steve') appears only if you damage the Holy Mountain, and hits as hard as anything in the game. Provoking a guardian by vandalism is a gag many games share (shopkeepers, guards, angels).
What it is there: A flying skeletal guard that spawns when the Holy Mountain's protected brickwork is damaged: 600 health, very high damage; 'Mall Cop' to the community.

Name: Ponzu
Goal: Defeat an enemy by hitting one specific spot
Why this pairing: Ponzu can only be hurt through the crystal on one of his necks; everything else is armour. The goal first drafted (blind) for Selt belongs here.
What it is there: Scaled Assembly, the Shimmering Caverns boss: heads rise out of four pits, a new one each quarter of his health, headbutting the walls to summon Scales.
Builds on: Hades' many-headed candidate is about the heads; this is about the weak spot

Name: Noori
Goal: Light a torch
Why this pairing: The four torches in Noori's room set its armour: each one out takes 25% off your damage, all four out and it takes none. Relighting them is the fight.
What it is there: Spectre of Darkness, the Halls of Din's boss: it snuffs the torches, opens portals for a hand to strike through, and fires cursed homing orbs.

Name: Mortar
Goal: Defeat a boss with a bomb
Why this pairing: Mortar can only be hurt directly by bombs; anything else has to go through his orbs or arms. UnderMine is a bomb game, and the board has bombs.
What it is there: Charged Golem, the Delvemore Dungeon's boss: a lightning golem that slams its arms down and sends orbs out that electrify the water.

Name: Din, the Old King
Goal: Defeat a character who helped you earlier in the same game
Why this pairing: Din is Arkanos, the archmage who greets you at the mine and sends you down it; at half health he drops the act. A friend turning out to be the last boss is a common twist.
What it is there: The true final boss: after the five bosses' stones are collected, Arkanos becomes Din, a giant hurt only through the crystal in his ribcage, who sweeps you into the void.

Name: Ogre Annihilator
Goal: Defeat an enemy with its own weapon
Why this pairing: The Annihilator is immune to everything but his own bombs, knocked back at him. 'Its own weapon' covers a thrown bomb, a dropped sword or a stolen gun; plain reflection is already Host's goal.
What it is there: A Shimmering Caverns ogre that walks the room then throws one to three Rook's Bombs that explode in a plus shape.

Name: Hoarding Pilfer
Goal: Defeat a treasure creature before it gets away
Why this pairing: A golden slime that drops gold every time it's hit and leaves after a while; ten hits before it goes pays a Blessing. The treasure goblin is a genre fixture. (The plain Pilfer, which steals dropped gold, is covered by two live goals: Giggling Minister's and Leprechaun's.)
What it is there: A rare golden Pilfer (5% a floor) that drops Gold and Thorium when hit instead of stealing, hides in chests, and leaves on a timer.
Clones: Scrounger (Ring of Pain): a treasure-dropping creature that walks one space toward the exit every 4 turns and leaves the floor if it gets there; Loot Bug (Deep Rock Galactic: Survivor): a harmless grub full of gold that never fights back or runs; Chrysoid (Returnal): a golden, harmless creature full of currency that runs and burrows away after a few seconds; Treasure Plane (Octogeddon): never attacks and pays coins every time it is hit as well as when it goes down

Name: Spectral Blade
Goal: Let a summon land the killing blow
Why this pairing: Your own Staff of Conjuration summons spectral blades too, and they fight for you until they flicker out. The goal first drafted for the Goblin Conjurer, on the body it was really about.
What it is there: A flickering, ethereal weapon that swarms, levitates and fades after a while; summoned by goblin conjurers and by the staff of conjuration.

Name: Phylactery
Goal: Destroy the thing keeping an enemy alive
Why this pairing: Kill a Lich and it reverts into a Phylactery; leave it and it becomes a Lich again. The Phoenix and its egg work the same way.
What it is there: The vessel a slain Lich turns into: helpless, but if not destroyed quickly it rises as a Lich again.

Name: Acid Mound
Goal: Take off your weapon to fight an enemy
Why this pairing: Every hit on an acid mound corrodes your weapon, so Brogue players unequip it and punch; the game even warns you before you swing.
What it is there: A mostly harmless blob that corrodes your weapon when you hit it and your armour when it hits you, a point of enchantment each time.

Name: Goblin Warlord
Goal: Defeat a boss that runs from you
Why this pairing: The warlord isn't threatening himself: he summons goblins, mystics and conjurers to fight for him and flees whenever he can.
What it is there: The boss of a Goblin Warren, guarding rare items such as keys; he summons goblin packs and runs.
Clones: Kowa the Coward (Shogun Showdown): a boss who runs from you and puts the enemies he spawns between you and him; Balrog (Red Rogue): the final boss holds the Amulet of Yendor and flees to the stairs, so the fight is cutting him off

Name: Mama Tick
Goal: Skip a boss fight
Why this pairing: Her fight can be skipped altogether by sacrificing the Mushroom Boi at the Swamp Priest's altar; attack her eye and it starts anyway.
What it is there: A tier 1 boss in the Nest (The Bad Seed DLC): a giant tick in the water, only her eye showing at first, hiding her body as she takes damage.

Name: The Servants
Goal: Climb ahead of rising fire to the top of a level
Why this pairing: The Lighthouse burns from the bottom as you climb it, with Calliope, then Euterpe, then Kleio chasing you up and stopping you to fight.
What it is there: Three bosses (The Queen and the Sea DLC), one per stat (Survival, Tactics, Brutality), fought on the way up the burning Lighthouse to the Queen.

Name: Gold Gorger
Goal: Defeat an enemy made of gold
Why this pairing: They absorb dropped gold to grow into stronger forms behind a force field, then drop every coin they ate.
What it is there: Golden enemies of the Bank, with stolen tridents and swords; 50 gold makes their second form, 300 their third.

Name: Beetle Queen
Goal: Defeat a queen
Why this pairing: The queen of the Beetle family, who calls Beetle Guards to her and fires acid that leaves burning pools.
What it is there: A teleporter boss that spits arcs of acid, summons Beetle Guards and leaves lingering acid pools.

Name: Wandering Vagrant
Goal: Hide behind something to survive an attack
Why this pairing: Its Genesis Supernova fills the area; the way through is to break line of sight behind terrain.
What it is there: A returning jellyfish boss that fires orb volleys and a slow homing orb bomb, and charges a supernova you can only hide from.

Name: Hermit Crab
Goal: Knock an enemy off the edge of the map
Why this pairing: The challenge 'The Demons And The Crabs' asks you to chase 20 Hermit Crabs off the map's edge. Push is a verb here.
What it is there: A ground mortar that buries itself to fire volleys from a distance; any hit over half its health stuns it.

Name: Graveyard Golem
Goal: Sneak past a sleeping enemy without waking it
Why this pairing: The Wandering Graveyard shuffles about until it naps; asleep it's harmless, woken early it rampages. The wiki's advice is to tiptoe round it.
What it is there: The Graveyard map's third-rank boss: a golem of countless corpses with a cemetery on its back that shakes undead loose to join the attack.

Name: Monkey King
Goal: Tell the real enemy apart from its illusions
Why this pairing: He floods the field with illusions so your gaze chases false threats while his monkeys raid the kingdom. Create an Illusion is already a live goal; this is the other side.
What it is there: A Shifting Sands boss: a rebellious trickster who lets no one else call himself king on his mountain.

Name: O'Cthulupus
Goal: Defeat a pirate
Why this pairing: Part pirate, part eldritch horror, with cannons bolted to his tentacles; between volleys he drags away supplies and weapons.
What it is there: The Dark Realm's first-rank boss, who fires on your units and steals from the kingdom.

Name: Smokeeye
Goal: Defeat a sniper
Why this pairing: A mercenary sharpshooter with a rifle 'welded together during a tantrum'; he stuns your troops with smoke, runs, and rings himself with spikes.
What it is there: The Volcano's first-rank boss, hired by the Scarlet Goblins.

Name: Unholy Crones
Goal: Defeat a witch
Why this pairing: Four sisters chasing necromancy and eternal youth, whose sibling rivalry keeps undermining their plans.
What it is there: The Graveyard's second-rank boss: four crones, one flying, one in melee and two casting, each dealing its own kind of damage.

Name: Trigger Twins
Goal: Defeat a pair of twins
Why this pairing: Smiley and Shades share the fight; kill one and the other flies into a rage with new attacks.
What it is there: A Keep of the Lead Lord boss: two Bullet Kin brothers who charge, summon Bullet Kin and fire their own signature attacks.
Clones: Orpheus and Erudyce (Barony): the sibling Archmagisters fought together at the end, a fire-and-melee brother and an ice-and-ranged sister

Name: HM Absolution
Goal: Go back to your character's past and change it
Why this pairing: Every Gungeoneer comes to the Gungeon to kill their past; the Pilot's ends at the HM Absolution, the warship he fled, leaving his friend Z behind.
What it is there: The Imperial Hegemony's warship in the Pilot's past, reached with the Bullet That Can Kill The Past.

Name: Star Spawn
Goal: Defeat a creature from the Cthulhu mythos
Why this pairing: Its name and design come straight from H. P. Lovecraft, and eldritch horrors from his stories turn up across games.
What it is there: The Champion of the Forbidden Fortress: a stronger monster with more Poise and two turns a round.

Name: Ravager
Goal: Defeat a wendigo
Why this pairing: Inspired by the Wendigo of Algonquian folklore, the spirit of insatiable hunger, which many games borrow.
What it is there: The alternative Champion of the Pilgrimage Path.

Name: Wolpertinger
Goal: Defeat a horned or winged rabbit
Why this pairing: The Bavarian wolpertinger: a small mammal, usually a hare, with wings, antlers and fangs. Killer and horned rabbits turn up in plenty of games. (Not 'a creature stitched from animals', which Curse of the Dead Gods' candidate already is.)
What it is there: A Wind monster of the Pilgrimage Path and the Fortress's first zone; its Memento comes free with the Cherufe starter.

Name: Mandragora
Goal: Defeat a mandrake
Why this pairing: The mandrake, the root shaped like a small person, from European and Middle Eastern folklore; it turns up as an enemy or an ingredient in many games.
What it is there: An Ambush monster in the Pilgrimage Path's second and third zones, staggered by Fire.

Name: Kid
Goal: Hatch a monster from an egg
Why this pairing: Kid is the infant dragon you hatch yourself: 'it can be tamed by the person who hatched its egg', and becomes a Dragon at level 20. Azure Dreams' familiars all come from eggs found in the tower and hatched in the Monster Hut. (Into the Breach's candidate is the opposite: destroying one.)
What it is there: A Fire monster never met in the Monster Tower: the infant form of the Dragon, with a severe temper.

Name: The Moon
Goal: Defeat the moon
Why this pairing: The last boss of the Vast Void is the moon itself. Fighting a moon (or something wearing its face) happens in more games than you'd think. ('Go to a Moon' is a live goal; this is fighting one.)
What it is there: The final boss of The VASTxVOID.

Name: Alarm-bot
Goal: Stop an enemy before it raises the alarm
Why this pairing: It does no damage at all: its whole job is to alert its surroundings and the ScourgeBringer's defences to an intruder. Alarms are a stealth staple; Cogmind's candidate is about not being seen at all.
What it is there: A bot that flies around a room raising the alarm when it detects you, very vulnerable to stuns while it does.

Name: Judge CandleMask
Goal: Attack a boss from its blind spot
Why this pairing: Its own description: 'The one who lays candles. Always be in its blind spot.'
What it is there: The second Judge, of the Still Bastion: it sweeps vertical and horizontal lasers across the room and fires bullets from the candles it spreads.

Name: Shinobo
Goal: Defeat a ninja
Why this pairing: A purple monkey in a red headband whose skills are a Kung Flip, a Drowsy kung fu strike, a flurry of shuriken and the Kung Fury super move.
What it is there: A Zen Zone beast; a Jumbo Shinobo is the boss of the Shinobo Lair.

Name: Nachzehrer
Goal: Stop an enemy from eating a corpse
Why this pairing: Nachzehrers eat corpses, even their own kind's, to grow a size, heal fully and lift their morale; the wiki's advice is to stand on the corpses yourself or spearwall them.
What it is there: A ghoulish beast of the plains and steppes, in three sizes; the largest can swallow a man whole.

Name: Alp
Goal: Wake an ally an enemy put to sleep
Why this pairing: Alps put your men to sleep, then feed them nightmares that hurt and wake them; you can spend a turn shaking a brother awake.
What it is there: A pale nighttime beast found everywhere but forests, swamps and hills, and in 'Ending the Nightmare' contracts.

Name: Hexe
Goal: Defeat the enemy that charmed your ally
Why this pairing: A Hexe's Charm turns one of your brothers against you for two turns, and it ends early only if she's dead. (Cogmind's candidate is watching it happen; this is ending it.)
What it is there: A witch guarded by beasts or brigands she has charmed, who also casts Hex.

Name: Unhold
Goal: Defeat a giant
Why this pairing: Unholds are the giants of Battle Brothers, hunted in 'Hunting Giants' contracts; there are regular, Bog and Frost Unholds, and armoured ones.
What it is there: A huge, regenerating brute of the hills, tundras and mountains.

Name: The Ghost
Goal: Leave a level before an unbeatable enemy comes for you
Why this pairing: It appears if you linger on a level (about two and a half minutes), has 9999 health and kills on touch: it exists to stop greedy treasure hunters loitering. (Named 'The Ghost', as the wiki writes it, because Crypt of the NecroDancer's Ghost is already a candidate.)
What it is there: The ultimate danger in Spelunky, which you can play the whole game without ever seeing.

Name: King Yama
Goal: Defeat the king of hell
Why this pairing: The ruler of Hell, the largest enemy in the game, with his henchmen Horse Head and Ox Face; beaten, his face tears off his skull and keeps fighting.
What it is there: The true final boss, on the last level of Hell (5-4), reached only through the City of Gold.

Name: Yeti King
Goal: Survive an avalanche
Why this pairing: His roar brings ice blocks crashing down from the ceiling and can blast you through the air.
What it is there: The Ice Caves' mini-boss, found in Yeti Kingdom levels with a guard of Yetis.

Name: The Brohannes
Goal: Play as the villain
Why this pairing: The secret final boss: Johannes's two brothers, and for this fight you don't play your hero, you play Johannes, the traitor himself.
What it is there: A remix boss reached through any boss gate after giving Charon the Traitor's Obol; beating it unlocks the Traitor class.
Clones: Octogeddon (Octogeddon): the hero is the monster, a mutant octopus wrecking human landmarks in revenge for sushi

Name: Darkling
Goal: Defeat a group of enemies that revive each other, all at once
Why this pairing: Darklings come in threes and a dead one comes back unless all three die together: you have to finish them in the same turn.
What it is there: Act 3 enemies that harden, nip and reincarnate while any Darkling still stands.

Name: Thanatos
Goal: Beat a rival to the most kills in one fight
Why this pairing: Death himself sometimes appears at the start of an encounter and challenges Zagreus to see who can slay more shades; he can't be hurt during the contest.
What it is there: The personification of Death, Nyx's son and Hypnos's twin, and Zagreus's oldest friend.

Name: Hades
Goal: Defeat your own father
Why this pairing: The whole game is an escape from the house of your father, who waits at the Temple of Styx's exit as the final boss.
What it is there: The god of the Underworld, master of the House, Zagreus's father and the main antagonist.

Name: Dreaming General
Goal: Defeat an enemy before it wakes up
Why this pairing: He is locked in a nightmare slumber and never wakes; the wiki's own line is 'End his suffering, and grant his soul the rest he longs for'.
What it is there: The Cadaver lair boss of the Tangle, an armoured colossus asleep in his keep, with a Tap Root that forces heroes to act out his nightmare.

Name: Librarian
Goal: Destroy the cover an enemy is hiding behind
Why this pairing: He starts the fight behind three stacks of books, and burning them down is what opens him up (and sets him alight).
What it is there: The Fanatic lair boss of the Sprawl, teetering on a moving ladder in the Great Library, burning books and flinging the pages.
Builds on: Hoplite's 'Use an enemy as cover' is the other side of it

Name: Leviathan
Goal: Break off part of a boss before you defeat it
Why this pairing: A two-part fight: the Leviathan's Hand drags a hero into the sea, and destroying the hand frees them, until it is summoned again.
What it is there: The Fisherfolk lair boss of the Shroud, at the Sacred Pier: 'They must be made to see that their monstrous god is mortal.'

Name: The Shackles of Denial
Goal: Beat a boss using only one kind of attack
Why this pairing: Each round one of its chains Denies a whole kind of skill (melee, ranged, healing or stress), so you fight it with what you are left with.
What it is there: The final boss of the Denial confession, the world's mind chained by its own command.

Name: Implication
Goal: Defeat an enemy while it is reloading
Why this pairing: A massive cannon that must reload between every shot, which is the window the wiki tells you to use.
What it is there: A Pillager enemy: a slow cannon that hits the whole party and misses often, with heavy armour in between shots.

Name: Special Offer
Goal: Haggle a shop's price down
Why this pairing: The fight's objective is not the boss but the item floating about the room: you shoot its price down from 999,999 debris.
What it is there: A secret Seal fight against a mech-riding Bloke, started by buying his Seal in Bloke's Shop after Overlord falls.

Name: Database
Goal: Defeat a boss made of two earlier bosses
Why this pairing: Between its four phases it sends one of 8 fusions of bosses from earlier floors at you.
What it is there: The boss of Nowhere, the secret seventh floor: a mechanical apparatus over stone-cased server towers, its arena glitching as the fight goes on.

Name: Lucid Dream
Goal: Win a fight without defeating every enemy in it
Why this pairing: Three crystals, three enemies (a mage, an Angel and a bat-like mech), and on Normal you only have to beat two of them, in the order you choose.
What it is there: A Loop boss on Floor 4, only on Loop 7 and up.
Clones: Black Bishop (Shotgun King: The Final Checkmate): a secret boss you only meet by leaving exactly one bishop alive when you kill the White King

Name: Whorl
Goal: Drown an enemy
Why this pairing: Drowning 20 Whorls is the achievement 'Sleepin' With The...', which unlocks an item.
What it is there: A carapaced flier with a short slowing beam; the field notes' explorer nearly had their suit cracked by one.

Name: Clown
Goal: Defeat a clown
Why this pairing: Clowns are the Dark Carnival's foot soldiers: the Ringmaster calls in four at three-quarters health, and Clown Jeremy fights with a Fool's Banjo.
What it is there: A family of creatures in the Dark Carnival, FtK2's endless mode of floors.
Clones: Pierrot (Dead Estate): THE FRAGILE FOOL, a clown boss bouncing on a rainbow ball, then crying tear bullets on foot

Name: Queen Rosomon
Goal: Overthrow a ruler
Why this pairing: The whole campaign is a resistance against her: she is the boss of the final area, the Castle Gates.
What it is there: The mad queen of Fahrul, a four-tile boss with a staff who summons two Chaos Beasts once hurt enough.

Name: Metal Patriarch
Goal: Defeat the pilot hiding inside a machine
Why this pairing: A Beak Lord that has infested a large metal shell; its chest armour opens after each laser and you shoot the Beak Lord hiding inside before it closes.
What it is there: The boss of the Factory: shoulder cannons, homing missiles and a head-mounted laser.

Name: Polyphemus
Goal: Blind an enemy
Why this pairing: Shoot its red eye and you blind it, which opens its two weak points; the strategy is to do it again and again.
What it is there: A boss of the Buried City: a floating, shelled orb of meat with eyes on every side, which breaks out of its shell when hurt enough.

Name: False Beast
Goal: Defeat an illusion by destroying what projects it
Why this pairing: An illusionary Mouth Meat that cannot be damaged at all; hit its Projector and it charges you until the Projector is destroyed.
What it is there: An enemy summoned by a False Beast Projector, which the Thief orb can also spawn by mistake.

Name: The Porcupine
Goal: Defeat an enemy that hurts you when you hit it
Why this pairing: Her wings were clipped and regrew so many times that her back is all spines: 'Don't touch my back!'
What it is there: A Clipped boss of Ring 4 who refuses to give up her wings.

Name: The Last Divinity
Goal: Defeat a boss that fills the whole battlefield
Why this pairing: It spans all three floors of the train and attacks every floor every turn, with Sweep on the top, Multistrike in the middle and Trample at the bottom.
What it is there: The DLC's true final boss in Ring 9, after Seraph, if you collected 100 Pact Shards (or always in Hell Rush).

Name: Jotun, Who Parts Limbs
Goal: Lose a limb and keep fighting
Why this pairing: His name says it: a legendary troll who dual-wields two-handed carbide battle axes, and in Qud a limb can come off.
What it is there: The first of three legendary trolls in the healing pools of Bethesda Susa.

Name: Girsh Qas
Goal: Defeat a boss whose death makes the rest stronger
Why this pairing: Kill Qas and every remaining Girsh gains +25 Quickness; pacify her with the water ritual instead and they don't.
What it is there: One of the six Girsh Nephilim, found with Girsh Qon under their chuppah, three strata down the Moon Stair.

Name: Jester
Goal: Defeat an enemy that comes back stronger every time you beat it
Why this pairing: The Jester levels up each time it is defeated, and changes its equipment every turn; beating it is how the sixth contestant unlocks.
What it is there: A unique enemy and the announcer for the first part of the game.

Name: Wicker Man
Goal: Set a scarecrow or a straw man on fire
Why this pairing: Made of wicker, weak to fire, and cheerful about it: 'I'll just weave myself back together again... Maybe this time I'll weave myself longer legs!'
What it is there: A level-4 enemy who came into the dungeons on a voyage of self-discovery.

Name: Violette
Goal: Dodge attacks that come in time with the music
Why this pairing: The only boss whose attacks are bound to the rhythm of her theme; syncopated sections make the attacks come faster.
What it is there: One of the playable heroes, fought as a boss when you aren't playing her.

Name: Terra
Goal: Win a fight while the floor breaks away under you
Why this pairing: Her fight is built on Break tiles that shrink the space you have to dodge in, with spinners that turn when they hit a broken tile.
What it is there: A playable hero fought as a boss.

Name: Terrable
Goal: Spare every boss you beat in a run
Why this pairing: She is only fought at the end of the Pacifist route, which you reach by sparing the bosses instead of executing them; she opens by destroying the Gate.
What it is there: The Pacifist route's final boss. Diablo's 'Spare an enemy that begs for its life' (candidate) is the single-enemy version.

Name: Gemini
Goal: Defeat a boss named after your own star sign
Why this pairing: The twelve bosses are the Zodiacs, each a star sign; any of them could carry this goal, and Gemini, the twins, is the one most players can name.
What it is there: A Zodiac of the Crimson Highlands; Zodiacs can also be summoned, set challenges and be chosen as an affinity.

Name: Big Bandit
Goal: Defeat a boss in under 10 seconds
Why this pairing: Kill him in less than 10 seconds and a portal opens to a secret area, the Oasis.
What it is there: The first boss, who jumps out of a wall in the Desert after you kill a tenth of the enemies on 1-3.

Name: The Nuclear Throne
Goal: Sit on a throne
Why this pairing: A skeleton sits on the throne at the end of a long red carpet, and you can't climb up to it; the whole game is the race to take its seat.
What it is there: The Palace's final boss: the throne itself, which grows legs, fires its beam (walking the carpet sets it off) and ends your run when beaten.

Name: Invoker
Goal: Escape a ring of bullets closing in around you
Why this pairing: Every two seconds it primes an area of projectiles around you that lands a second later; each phase widens it, and in the last it races around the arena drawing a circle of projectiles around you. Getting out of the ring before it lands is the fight. (Moonlighter's Golem King, a candidate, already has the shadow-on-the-ground dodge.)
What it is there: One of Brotato's wave-20 bosses: a 15,000-health caster that fills the arena with primed projectile zones.

Name: Shapeshifter
Goal: Find an enemy disguised as a harmless person
Why this pairing: A Shapeshifter rides inside a random NPC who acts normally for their kind; the only tell is the red eyes, which glasses can hide. Once its host dies it pops out and runs, and it drops a lot of money, so hunting it pays. Mimics (candidates) pose as objects; this one poses as a person.
What it is there: An NPC and playable character, the smallest in the game, that possesses other people's bodies.

Name: Mayor
Goal: Take a ruler's hat or crown
Why this pairing: The run ends when you take the Mayor's Hat; the Mayor wears it, is always on the minimap with 'GET HAT' over their head, and is never far from their security detail. How you get it (kill, steal, trick) is up to you.
What it is there: The primary antagonist, found only in Mayor Village, doing one of seven things (sleeping, swimming, dancing...).

Name: Nekosh
Goal: Defeat a boss that reveals its true form
Why this pairing: Nekosh is a small spellcaster until you beat him; then he tricks you into releasing his true form from the book he carries, a fire demon with two scythes. A boss that turns out to be something else is a staple of action games.
What it is there: Nekosh - Keeper of the Books, the librarian and main boss of the Obsidian Cathedral, guarding its blasphemous archive.

Name: Hezek
Goal: Defeat an enemy that breaks free of its chains
Why this pairing: Hezek is chained to the wall by one wrist; in his second phase he tears his own arm off to chase you. Chained beasts that get loose are a familiar boss beat.
What it is there: Hezek - The Baptized, the masked brute with a spiked club who guards the Bloodied Paths: normally the first boss outside the tutorial.

Name: Dwarf monk
Goal: Get your weapon knocked out of your hands
Why this pairing: Monks strike twice for every attack you make and keep knocking the Hero's weapon to the floor, sometimes again and again as you pick it back up. Disarming is a classic roguelike trick, and losing your weapon mid-fight is something most games can do to you.
What it is there: A Dwarven City enemy, fast martial artists; 1 in 30 spawns as a Senior monk.

Name: Gnoll shaman
Goal: Break line of sight to draw a ranged enemy in close
Why this pairing: Shamans throw lightning from a distance and are weak up close; the wiki's advice is to hide behind a door so it has to come to you, into melee. Fighting around corners is the oldest tactic in turn-based roguelikes.
What it is there: A Sewers enemy, a gnoll caster with a powerful ranged lightning bolt and a feeble melee attack.

Name: Mana Devourer
Goal: End a turn with nothing left unspent
Why this pairing: Its Mana Hunger eats every die you leave unused at the end of a turn, and each one makes it stronger. Every deckbuilder has a resource that resets each turn (energy, mana, dice); spending all of it is the discipline this enemy punishes you for lacking.
What it is there: A Void enemy that hits for 20 and Silences, and every few turns makes your spells lose charges.

Name: Heart of the Forest
Goal: Stun an enemy by hitting it hard enough in one blow
Why this pairing: It starts with 25 Delicate: take that much Health off it in one go and it is Stunned; the threshold grows by 10 each turn, so the hit has to come early and big. Saving up for one huge hit is the deckbuilder fantasy.
What it is there: A Deadwoods boss that summons two Roots of the Forest to its front and rear when it is alone.

Name: Snarfrattle
Goal: Hunt down a beast someone has sworn revenge on
Why this pairing: Snarfrattle only exists if you take the Kill Hyena quest from a vengeful one-armed hunter at the port (a nod to Moby-Dick), and it comes with two or three hyenas. Hunting a named beast for someone else is a quest most strategy and adventure games offer.
What it is there: A unique black hyena, much stronger than a normal one; in RIVALS it wanders as an uncommon enemy instead.

Name: One Punch
Goal: Take an enemy's strongest blow and stay standing
Why this pairing: Its whole bio is the goal: 'Anyone who can withstand a punch from Tomozou will be respected as a real man by him.' Every strategy game has an enemy with one huge telegraphed attack; letting it land and living is the dare.
What it is there: A bounty: Tomozou, a 'creepy bald guy' with a cute granddaughter, and one punch.

Name: Possum Player
Goal: Defeat an enemy that was only playing dead
Why this pairing: 'You thought he was dead!' It only appears out of the Playing Possum event: the body you walked past gets up. Enemies that fake their death turn up across games, and spotting one is the trick.
What it is there: A beast with 40 HP that spawns from the Playing Possum event.

Name: Knight of the Flame
Goal: Win a fight after losing your strongest unit or card
Why this pairing: Its power Cull the Strong destroys your follower with the highest attack at the start of every one of your turns, so the fight is won by everything except your best piece. Every deckbuilder has a carry; losing it and winning anyway is the dare.
What it is there: The boss guarding the Shiram Monastery, with Legendary Foe (a piece of legendary equipment added to the rewards).

Name: Ambas Worm
Goal: Land the finishing blow with your weakest card or unit
Why this pairing: Ferocious Underdog: at the start of each of your turns the follower with the lowest attack, yours or its, gains +2 attack, so the smallest thing on the field keeps growing. Winning with the underdog is its whole joke.
What it is there: A boss protecting the Abandoned Dam, a random location: 23 health and 0 armour at level 7.

Name: Replicator
Goal: Defeat an enemy before the weapons it keeps adding outgun you
Why this pairing: Dillian's tiny ship sprouts two new cannons every turn, 'slowly creating a wall of destruction', so the wiki's advice is a swift kill. A clock that ticks by the enemy growing is a shape every deckbuilder has (scaling enemies, Slay the Spire's Cultist).
What it is there: DPL-55555 "Replicator", a 3-tile ship with two cockpits and one cannon to start, 8 hull and 14 shields.

Name: Mysterious Tree
Goal: Defeat an enemy far too tough to wear down, with something that hurts by a share of its health
Why this pairing: An immobile tree with 45,000 health, more than any boss, so normal weapons barely dent it; Frostbite, which deals a percentage of max health, kills it easily. Percentage damage against a damage sponge is a trick from Pokémon's Super Fang to Souls bleed builds.
What it is there: An immobile enemy in the Forest map.

Name: Time Weaver
Goal: Beat a game without reloading a save
Why this pairing: It only appears if you continue or reload twice on the same floor: a Blocker with humongous stats and piercing damage, 'essentially a consequence for attempting to abuse the save system'. Save-scumming is possible in nearly every game, so refusing it is a goal anyone can hold to.
What it is there: A unique creature that exists to punish reloading.

Name: Vran the Sullen
Goal: Defeat a leader before his followers fall
Why this pairing: Vran buffs his allies and lands a heavy attack whenever one of his companions dies, so the usual 'clear the minions first' makes him worse; the wiki's advice is to keep him stunned and decide the kill order. Kill order is the core puzzle of party battlers.
What it is there: A boss with the Unbridled Frenzy ability, fought with a tank, a damage dealer and a healer.

Name: Lemurian Cavalry
Goal: Knock a rider off its mount
Why this pairing: The one Lemurian that rides: a red-plumed lancer on a tamed Boarlit. Riders are everywhere (goblin wolf-riders, knights, Spelunky's mounts), and unhorsing one is a move a player makes on purpose. It is the other side of Qilin's 'Ride an animal'.
What it is there: A late-game enemy (Temple of the Elders, the final stage): a Lemurian in a helmet with a serrated spear, riding a domesticated, longer-tusked Boarlit.
Clones: Biker (Picayune Dreams): the stage 3 boss charging you down on a motorcycle, a vehicle rather than a mount

Name: Clay Man
Goal: Hit an enemy while hanging from a rope or a ladder
Why this pairing: Its wiki singles it out as one of only four enemies that climb ropes and attack from them. Ropes and ladders are a platformer staple, and fighting from one instead of waiting until you're down is a small, real feat in most Action games.
What it is there: A short man of black tar with an urn for a head and a golden sword; it rolls toward you, thrusts on a short cooldown, and follows you up ropes.

Name: Lynx Totem
Goal: Destroy an idol that enemies worship
Why this pairing: A walking stone idol, the centre of the Lynx Tribe's religion, with a shaman on top calling the faithful to defend it. Idols, totems and shrines that monsters gather round are in a great many games; smashing one is the goal. NetHack's Aligned Cleric is the opposite act ('Worship at an altar').
What it is there: A boss: a tall foliage-covered stone totem on two stubby legs, animated by the Lynx shaman riding it. It summons four Lynx Tribe members and is the only boss that jumps.

Name: Severed
Goal: Defeat an enemy that followed you out of its room
Why this pairing: Its teleport leaves a red trail and makes it one of the only hostiles a closed area door doesn't stop: leaving the room doesn't end the fight. Pursuers that break the room rule are a fixture (Resident Evil's Mr. X, Isaac's Hush-style chasers), and finishing one off after it chased you is the feat.
What it is there: A blade-armed hostile of the Crimson Wastes. It walks, then slams its blade into the ground to teleport around the arena, and is always staggered at half health.

Name: Crab
Goal: Defeat 3 crabs
Why this pairing: The most basic enemy of a game that is all crabs: it looks exactly like the player, without a weapon. Crabs are a stock enemy far beyond it (Terraria, Zelda's Sand Crabs, Hollow Knight, Risk of Rain), and a counted Bounty is how the live sheet does a common body (Fat Gremlin, Blobulin).
What it is there: Crabs spawn in small groups from the start, in every biome but the Ice Biome; they walk straight at you and jump when close, attacking with their claws.

Name: Locust
Goal: Keep pests off something you planted or grew
Why this pairing: Locusts don't come for you, they come for the crops, and a crop knocked free is a race back to save it. Pests, raiders and crows on the garden are in every farming and tower-defence game; protecting what you grew is the feat.
What it is there: A night-time farm enemy (also called Fruit Flies) that spawns in a group, flies to the nearest crop and eats it until it is destroyed, returning faster if knocked away.

Name: Tree Monster
Goal: Follow a glowing guide to something hidden
Why this pairing: You never stumble on a Tree Monster: a Golden Pupa turns into a firefly and leads you to where it rises. Wisps, fairies and fireflies that lead the way are everywhere (Zelda's Navi, Ori, will-o'-the-wisps); following one to the end is the goal.
What it is there: A miniboss ('Tree Guardian'), one per biome area. A Golden Pupa, dropped at random by a cleared camp, becomes a firefly that leads you to the spot where the Tree Monster spawns; it drops Golden Pupa loot.

Name: Barakunarash
Goal: Stay on a level so long that something worse comes for you
Why this pairing: A Baron is what you get for lingering: the Quasimorphosis meter climbs with time and every death on the floor, and at 1000 a storm breaks and the bramfatura's Baron walks in. Spelunky's ghost, Isaac's time-out angels and Dead Cells' timed doors all punish staying too long; this asks you to stay anyway.
What it is there: The Barakunarash are the Barons of Ur, armed with the Ninurtagun, a quasimorphic rocket launcher that is their arm (amputate it to wield it). A Baron enters when the meter reaches 1000, beginning the Rapture phase.
Clones: Hunter's Mark (Mortal Sin): an optional curse under which an immortal pursuer appears if you stay in a level too long, in exchange for better drops

Name: Baron Herx
Goal: Defeat a villain who has been taunting you all game
Why this pairing: Herx gets into your head from the first floor, musing on your progress and turning hostile as you near him. The villain on the intercom (GLaDOS, Handsome Jack, SHODAN, Herx) is a fixture, and finally shutting one up is the goal.
What it is there: The antagonist: a greedy baron the people of Hamlet locked in the Mines with the promise of gold. He made a pact with Baphomet, became a lich, and talks into your mind all the way down to Herx's Lair.

Name: Jack
Goal: Find a safe path through a field of bombs or mines
Why this pairing: In his Jack-O'-Bomb field he sits in a far corner behind a maze of pumpkin bombs with exactly one safe path to him. Minefields with one way through are in Minesweeper, war shooters and platformers alike, and the live BroomSweeper is one; crossing one untouched is the feat.
What it is there: The boss of the Botanical Ballroom: once a gardener with a love of comedy whose puns escalated into explosive pranks, obsessed with growing the ultimate pumpkin. He appears after 225 ghosts, between two pumpkin bombs; beating him earns 'Pumpkin Smasher'.

Name: Climber Slime
Goal: Defeat an enemy walking on the ceiling
Why this pairing: Its whole trick is flipping onto the underside of a floor and pacing the ceiling of the one below. Ceiling-crawlers (Metroid's Zoomers, Castlevania's spiders, Hollow Knight) are a platformer staple, and hitting one up there is a small, real feat.
What it is there: A spectral slime fused with a wraith's essence: faster than other slimes, twice the damage, and it flips to walk the roof of the floor it spawned on.

Name: Phantom King
Goal: Defeat 300 enemies in one game
Why this pairing: He only comes after you have destroyed 300 ghosts: the final room counts down to him. Body counts in the hundreds are normal in survivors-likes and hordes, rare elsewhere, which makes it a goal that reads very differently by game.
What it is there: The final boss and the mansion's cursed master (the Candy King). Once 300 ghosts are defeated Molli freezes and he appears, invulnerable at first, raising pillars of fire across all four floors.

Name: Kur
Goal: Defeat a boss, then use the power it leaves you on the next one
Why this pairing: Kur's Quint Laser is both its signature attack and the reward for beating it: every 20XX boss leaves its power behind, the Mega Man rule. Taking a boss's own weapon into the next fight is a staple far beyond Mega Man (Hollow Knight's spells, Kirby, Cuphead's charms).
What it is there: A dragonoid robot about twice the hero's size, one of two Skytemple bosses; its Quint Laser floats a neon square that explodes on impact, fired as a spread or a wall.

Name: Vile Visage
Goal: Defeat a boss too big to fit on the screen
Why this pairing: A giant face spanning the whole height of its room, firing from its mouth, eyes or forehead. Bosses that are only partly on screen (Contra, Gradius, Shadow of the Colossus) are a set piece of the genre.
What it is there: One of the Frostor bosses: a face filling the right side of the boss room, its attacks telegraphed by a blinking red eye at the part about to fire.

Name: The Glitch
Goal: Be fooled by a fake crash or a fake ending
Why this pairing: The Static Demon fakes an error message the moment you collect the Boss Key, as if it had crashed your game. Fourth-wall tricks (Pony Island, Inscryption, Doki Doki, Metal Gear's 'fake' game over) are a small genre of their own, and falling for one is the goal.
What it is there: The boss of the Old Set: a floating ghost of television static that 'holds some kind of mysterious power over the game itself', crashing it with a fake error and making minions out of static.

Name: Cow
Goal: Hunt an animal for its meat
Why this pairing: Cows exist only to be turned into Raw Meat: they never fight back and only run when hit (achievement: 'That's not very milk of you, sir', kill 250). Hunting game for food is in every survival game (Minecraft, Don't Starve, Valheim).
What it is there: A passive enemy in herds of up to five, the only enemy incapable of dealing damage; when attacked it doubles its speed and flees.

Name: Diver
Goal: Follow coordinates or a treasure map to what's buried there
Why this pairing: A secret boss reached only by a chain: blow up a Statue of Experience, take its floppy disk, read the coordinates it adds to the pause menu, and dig up the chest waiting there. Treasure maps (Sea of Thieves, Zelda, Red Dead) are everywhere; following one to the end is the goal.
What it is there: A submarine-piloting creature in search of treasure, added in the Contamination Update; the treasure chest at the coordinates summons him.

Name: Bankrupt Gambler
Goal: Lose a bet
Why this pairing: 'Driven by relentless misfortune, his every move fueled by desperation in fate's cruel game of ruin.' While he stands, every 1 you roll costs a Gold Coin. Bets and gambling minigames are in a great many games (Red Dead's poker, Yakuza's casinos, Dave the Diver's parlour); losing one is the goal. The Slice & Dice Gambler candidate asks the other way, to win one.
What it is there: An enemy card with two Exact-6 dice slots to fill and 6 damage; while unfolded, rolling a 1 loses you a Gold Coin.

Name: Goblin Shark
Goal: Catch an enemy alive instead of killing it
Why this pairing: Dave dives to catch fish for the sushi bar, and a tranquilized or netted catch is worth more than a dead one; the Goblin Shark is the mini-boss that tranquilizers were made for. Capturing alive (Monster Hunter's traps, Pokémon, Ark) is a real choice in many games.
What it is there: A depths fish and the mini-boss of the Chapter 3 sub-mission Curious Child: a shark up to 7 m long that shoots its jaws out to feed, vulnerable to the Tranquilizing Harpoon.

Name: The Interloper
Goal: Close a portal to stop what's coming through it
Why this pairing: A secret eldritch boss reached through a rift into the Mynasthar, the 'Mouth of Madness'; the fight turns on closing the rift, which can take its head off as it shuts. Sealing a portal (Doom, Diablo's hellgates, Oblivion's gates) is a goal many games set.
What it is there: An extra-dimensional, tentacled, Cthulhu-like abomination that the Black Cloaks' cult tries to contact, one of the toughest optional fights in the game.

Name: Dreadnought
Goal: Defeat a boss by hitting its weak point
Why this pairing: Its armour soaks everything but the command bridge, so the fight is finding and hitting that one spot. A glowing weak point (Zelda's eyes, Metroid's Mother Brain, Shadow of the Colossus) is one of the oldest boss designs there is.
What it is there: 'DREDNAUT': an extremely heavily armoured static air vessel brimming with turrets and runways, launching aircraft once you are within 1500; its weak point is the command bridge. Rare, from day 5 on.

Name: Turtle
Goal: Defeat an enemy by jumping on it
Why this pairing: Bullets and explosions from above glance off its shell, so the only way through is your own boots. Stomping is the oldest attack in games (Mario, Sonic, Shovel Knight's pogo) and nothing asks for it yet.
What it is there: A Caverns and Aquifer enemy that walks the walls (or swims in World 3); it 'cannot be killed from above via bullets or explosions due to their shells, and must be stomped in order to be killed'.

Name: Burlypup
Goal: Defeat something adorable
Why this pairing: 'Will disarm you with its cuteness, then flatten you with a huge club!' Its Cute card drains your attack. Cute enemies you have to bring yourself to hit (Pokémon, Kirby, Undertale's Froggits) are everywhere.
What it is there: An enemy of the Cliffs of Mythos whose deck mixes a delayed 8-damage Driftwood Club, a stunning Flipper Slap and Cute, which drains 3 attack energy.

Name: Fear
Goal: Defeat a boss that personifies an emotion
Why this pairing: Each of Cassidy's bosses is a feeling (Fear, Isolation, Loss, Negativity, Regret, Resentment). Emotions given a body to fight are a whole tradition: Psychonauts, Celeste's Badeline, Persona's Shadows, Sea of Solitude.
What it is there: The first biome's boss, a nightmare like a whale that lives in Cassidy's dream of her flooded hometown street; you beat it by baiting it into the mines in the arena.

Name: Krabken
Goal: Survive a boss fight until something else ends it
Why this pairing: Instead of a timer to run from, Krabken brings a Cataclysm: hold out long enough and the world kills it (or you). Survive-the-clock boss fights (Undertale's Asgore-likes, Terraria's events, Furi's last stand) are a staple.
What it is there: The final boss of every run, with no + versions; if enough time passes without Darwin or a charmed animal killing it, a Cataclysm starts that will eventually kill it, or Darwin.

Name: Undead Moose
Goal: Hit an enemy in the opening right after its attack
Why this pairing: Its headbutt and stun are the danger, and the reward is the moment after, when its head falls from its shoulders. Waiting out a big swing and punishing the recovery is the heart of Souls-likes and fighting games.
What it is there: A tree dungeon enemy: it rears up and butts (twice at higher levels), then tries a stun, after which 'the head falls from the shoulders and it is vulnerable'.

Name: The Brute
Goal: Hide from an enemy until it gives up looking for you
Why this pairing: None of Monstrum's three monsters can be killed: you duck into a locker or under a bed and wait, and a monster that checks a closed cupboard rips its door off. Hiding while something hunts you (Alien: Isolation, Amnesia, Outlast) is a genre of its own.
What it is there: The first and fastest of the three monsters that may stalk the Hisa Maru: a fiery behemoth that forces its way through anything, power-locked doors included.

Name: Abaddon
Goal: Learn a skill from an enemy you defeated
Why this pairing: Beat an elite in Crown Trick and it becomes a Familiar that lends you its skills. Taking a beaten enemy's power is a long tradition: Mega Man, Kirby, Final Fantasy's Blue Mages, Hollow Knight's charms.
What it is there: An elite (an armoured general who died in the forest of Bartland and was revived as the Witches' plaything); beaten, he joins the Ring of One as a Familiar.

Name: Demon Golem
Goal: Defeat an enemy that can only be hurt from a distance
Why this pairing: Brawler: 'Immune while the hero is on any of the cardinally adjacent squares.' So you can't just walk up and hit it, in a game where every move is a chess piece's. Enemies you have to fight at range are common, and nothing asks for one yet.
What it is there: A Foul Shrine enemy with Brawler, Void Grasp (in death it drags the hero the way the blow came) and Spark Surge (it strikes its squares after you cast a Cantrip).

Name: Wind Magistrate
Goal: Choose which boss to fight next, and beat it
Why this pairing: You pick the order of Battle Shapers' towers, and every Overlord gains a power each time you face one and each tower you free, so the order is the strategy. Choosing your boss (Mega Man's stage select, Hollow Knight's dreamers, Elden Ring's demigods) is a staple.
What it is there: One of the Overlords: once a political champion of the oppressed, she turned her mind to self-preservation; she rules a random tower each run and grows stronger with every tower you liberate.

Name: Cockroach
Goal: Defeat an enemy with exactly the damage it had left
Why this pairing: Resilient: if a hit would take its health below zero, it revives at full instead, so it has to be finished with an exact blow. Exact kills (Slay the Spire's lethal math, Balatro's score targets, a JRPG's last HP) are a puzzle many games set.
What it is there: An enemy with the Resilient Modifier (boxing gloves by its health): overkill it and it comes back to full health.
